lead: Algebraic laws let you rewrite regular expressions without changing the language they denote. They are useful when you need a shorter expression for a pattern, when you compare two expressions, or when you convert an expression to an automaton. Only a few universities teach these laws as a separate topic, but they appear in many exam solutions and in tools that optimise pattern matching.
prereq: You need: Regular expressions: operators and precedence.

blocks.text: An identity element does not change the language when it is concatenated. The empty string ε is the identity for concatenation. For any expression a, a·ε = a and ε·a = a. Both sides denote the same set of strings.
A null element makes the whole expression denote the empty language ∅. For any a, a·∅ = ∅ and ∅·a = ∅. The language on the left contains no strings, so the right side also contains none.
Idempotent law removes duplicate alternatives. (a|a) = a because the union of a language with itself is the same language. This law works for any expression a.

blocks.where: L(x) is the language described by expression x.

items: Use identity to drop unnecessary ε.
Use null to eliminate concatenations that can never produce a string.

blocks.text: Distributive law moves concatenation over union. a·(b|c) = a·b | a·c and (a|b)·c = a·c | b·c. Both sides generate exactly the same strings because each choice in the union is followed by the same concatenation.
Star law defines the Kleene closure. a* denotes zero or more repetitions of a. It satisfies a* = ε | a·a* and a* = ε | a*·a. The law shows that adding one more copy of a does not change the language.
a·(b|c) = a·b | a·c   (a|b)·c = a·c | b·c   a* = ε | a·a*
blocks.where: · is concatenation, | is union, * is Kleene star, ε is empty string.

items: Identify a part of the expression that matches the left side of a law.
Replace it with the right side.
Repeat until no further reduction is possible.

examples.question: Simplify the regular expression (a|b)*·a·(a|b)* using the algebraic laws.
steps: The expression has the form X·a·Y where X = (a|b)* and Y = (a|b)*.
No identity or null law applies because neither X nor Y is ε or ∅.
The idempotent law does not apply because the two (a|b)* are separated by a.
The distributive law cannot move a across the stars because star does not distribute over concatenation.
Therefore the expression cannot be reduced further.
examples.answer: The simplified expression is (a|b)*·a·(a|b)*; it is already in minimal form.

traps: Treating a·b* as (a·b)*; the star applies only to the preceding expression.
Assuming (a|b)*·ε = (a|b) without checking that ε is already included in the star.
Applying distributive law to a*·b as a*·b = (a·b)*; this is false.
Confusing the null law a·∅ = ∅ with the identity law a·ε = a.

quiz.q: What symbol denotes the empty language?
Explain why (a|a) = a holds for any expression a.
quiz.a: Both sides describe the same set of strings because the union of a language with itself adds no new strings.

quiz.q: Use the identity law to simplify a·ε·b.
quiz.a: First apply a·ε = a, giving a·b. No further reduction.

quiz.q: Given the expression (a·∅) | b, determine the language and show the steps.
quiz.a: a·∅ = ∅ by the null law, so the expression becomes ∅ | b = b. The language contains exactly the strings of b.

quiz.q: Show that a* = ε | a·a* using the star law.
quiz.a: By definition of Kleene star, a* includes the empty string ε and all strings formed by one a followed by any number of a's, i.e., a·a*.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, regular‑expression engines use these laws to optimise pattern matching, reducing backtracking and improving speed. Research on regex derivatives extends the algebraic approach to support look‑ahead and back‑references. Modern compilers for languages like Rust or JavaScript apply these rewrites automatically. To explore further, search for "regex derivative" and "automata‑based regex optimisation".
